chapters.headline: One 28 nm die, configured in firmware, becomes fifteen products.
chapters.lede: DeepGrid Semi's SoC2 is a single monolithic die on TSMC 28 nm HPC+ that fuses eleven sensor channels in 8.6 ms of a 33.3 ms frame budget, leaving 74% of that budget unused. That headroom means every SKU in the portfolio, from a one-camera mirror unit to a full ADAS kit, is a firmware and front-end change, not a new chip programme.
chapters.detail: The die is a monolithic design, not a chiplet assembly, comprising 64 compute cubes each containing 512 multiply-accumulate units, clocked at 600 MHz; the 39.3 TOPS INT8 figure is derived as 64 × 512 × 600 MHz × 2 ÷ 10¹², not rounded up. Memory bandwidth of 102.4 GB/s via dual-channel LPDDR5 is the binding constraint for multi-camera sensor fusion, not raw compute throughput. The architecture includes hardware softmax and weight-stationary attention, operations the Information Memorandum describes as infeasible at frame rate on an FPGA, alongside lockstep cores and a hardware root of trust as the stated path toward an automotive safety rating. The 8.6 ms fusion figure and the 39.3 TOPS figure are described as simulation and feasibility results; the Information Memorandum notes a PrimeSoC feasibility assessment dated March 2026, and the die has not yet been fabricated in 28 nm. Because every lower-channel configuration sits well within the frame budget, the fifteen-SKU portfolio is presented as one tapeout rather than fifteen separate chip programmes.

chapters.headline: Six domains on one die means six revenue lines from one tapeout.
chapters.lede: The ~57.1 mm² die is partitioned into six named compute domains, each targeting a distinct market and sold as its own product line. Because all six share a single tapeout, a competitor wishing to replicate the portfolio would need six separate tapeout programmes.
chapters.detail: The A100 houses 64 PCOREs × 512 MACs (32,768 MACs total, 39.3 TOPS INT8, architecture arithmetic and not a silicon measurement) and supports six-camera MIPI CSI-2, forming the core compute for all AD0–AD4 mobility kits. The R100 integrates a 12-bit native radar ADC for 77 GHz FMCW, 4D radar, and 60 GHz mmWave, with an FFT engine and CFAR detector; the Information Memorandum states the TI AWR2243 is fully eliminated in RTL. The T100 combines a LiDAR point cloud DSP with a thermal camera ISP (LWIR MIPI) and an ONNX runtime, targeting autonomous truck edge inference and an IP-licensing SaaS model described as carrying 90% margin. The D100 provides an AES-256 secure enclave, lockstep RISC-V targeting ASIL-B, and ECC SRAM for humanoid, UGV, and drone applications; the Information Memorandum states ₹1 Cr in institutional defence revenue was received in Q1 2026. The S100 handles vehicle networking via CAN FD ×4, Ethernet TSN (IEEE 802.1Qbv), AUTOSAR Adaptive, an OTA update engine, C-V2X/5G-NR, and AIS-140 telematics, while the H100 runs ECG, EEG, and SpO2 inference from a 24-bit bio-ADC at a design target of under 1 mW continuous, with driver-fatigue and AEB integration covered by Patent 14.

chapters.headline: Eleven sensor streams fuse in 8.6 ms, leaving 74% of the frame budget spare.
chapters.lede: DeepGrid Semi's in-cab compute part accepts seven RGB cameras, two thermal cameras and two radars, eleven configured inputs, and outputs a single fused AD2 perception stream. The reusable product is the compute and software platform; the sensor installation is one application of it, which matters commercially because the same semiconductor can serve multiple truck configurations.
chapters.detail: The seven RGB cameras are assigned distinct roles: road left and right, side left and right, a forward dashcam, a driver-monitoring camera and a rear camera. Each mirror tower combines a road-facing camera, a 120-degree side camera and a thermal camera, so the same quarter of the truck is observed in three different sensing modalities simultaneously. Front and rear 4D 77 GHz radars contribute range and relative-motion data at both ends of the vehicle, where cameras are weakest in rain and glare. The Information Memorandum (June 2026) states the design target is to fuse all eleven channels in 8.6 ms of the 33.3 ms frame, described as 74% headroom; the architecture illustration is labelled 'illustrative sensor-fusion timing, not a measured production latency.' The chip is not yet fabricated in 28 nm, so these figures require workload and implementation validation; calibration, occlusion, mounting tolerance and the final sensor bill of materials also remain to be confirmed.

passages.title: The compute box: 11 sensors in, AD2 out

chapters.headline: Key performance figures need staged hardware proof before investors should rely on them.
chapters.lede: DeepGrid Semi's 8.6 ms processing claim and TOPS arithmetic peaks are management figures derived from architecture illustrations, not measurements from fabricated silicon. Investor confidence should be released in stages, FPGA demonstration, ASIC verification, and vehicle qualification, each answering different questions and each requiring reproducible hardware evidence.
chapters.detail: The 8.6 ms figure is a management claim against a 33.3 ms frame budget (approximately 30 frames per second); the 24.7 ms remainder is budget subtraction, not measured system headroom, and the measurement boundary, which acquisition, inference, and fusion stages are included, has not been fixed. Two separate compute configurations appear in the source material: a 56-core configuration with a 34.4 TOPS arithmetic peak and a 64-core configuration with a 39.3 TOPS arithmetic peak, both at 600 MHz; neither figure represents measured application throughput, and the sources state the two configurations should not silently stand in for each other. The chip has not been fabricated in 28 nm and no silicon measurements exist; the sources describe the architecture as illustrative, not independently measured silicon evidence. The development plan distinguishes an existing FPGA platform, which exercises software, interfaces, and prototype compute, from the proposed production ASIC, which must separately verify scaled compute, memory, clock, power, and area together. A production advantage depends on the complete platform, compute, memory scheduling, compiler, and integration, and the sources state that arithmetic peaks alone do not establish it.

chapters.headline: Per-core data engines proposed to end the queue that stalls arithmetic units
chapters.lede: In the current shared-dispatch architecture, eight processing cores queue behind a single data-movement engine, leaving compute idle while data waits its turn. Replacing that bottleneck with an independent local DMA per core is the proposed fix, though results remain estimates awaiting testbench evidence.
chapters.detail: The shared-dispatch arrangement serialises data requests: all eight cores queue at one dispatch point, so adding more arithmetic units does not help when those units are waiting for data. The proposed local DMA design gives each core its own 16-entry descriptor table, a three-level address generator that walks tensor layouts without consulting a central dispatcher for every transfer, and a read FIFO that buffers arrivals between memory service and compute consumption. A frame-time reduction from 470 ms to 85 ms is cited as a proposal awaiting testbench evidence, the sources label it an estimate, not a measured result. The implementation cost is estimated at roughly 600 FPGA lookup tables per engine, or approximately 4,800 for eight engines before arbitration logic and firmware; these are engineering estimates, not finished implementation figures or production cost quotes, and the sources keep them distinct from any ASIC area or cost. Even with local dispatch, parallel requests still compete for finite shared memory-bank service capacity, and the sources note that differentiation would need to be demonstrated through workload results, compiler mapping and defensible implementation IP, not through the presence of a local DMA alone.

chapters.headline: Eight hardware layers multiply arithmetic positions eightfold, but the data path decides real throughput
chapters.lede: The 8×8×8 compute cube stacks eight 8×8 matrix layers to express reduction depth in hardware rather than software iteration, raising multiply-accumulate positions per cube from 64 to 512 in a single cycle. Two sources project different system-level arithmetic peaks depending on cube count, and both figures are design targets that require workload and implementation validation before they can be treated as measured results.
chapters.detail: The flat 8×8 array holds 64 multiply-accumulate positions and processes reduction depth across successive iterations; the 8×8×8 cube holds 512 positions and expresses that same depth in hardware, so all eight layers fire in one cycle. The 8× arithmetic ratio is an idealized comparison on the same K=8 tile at the same precision and is not an application speedup. The portfolio deck states a system arithmetic peak of 34.4 TOPS, derived from 56 cubes × 512 MACs × 600 MHz × 2 operations; the Information Memorandum states 39.3 TOPS, derived from 64 cubes × 512 MACs at 600 MHz. Both figures are arithmetic ceilings, not benchmarks, and both sources state that targets and arithmetic peaks require workload and implementation validation. Sustained useful work also depends on tensor layout, address distribution across the eight shared L2 banks, arbitration, and compiler scheduling: the sources illustrate that routing all 56 requests to a single bank stalls the array even while seven banks sit idle, making the data path a co-equal design constraint alongside compute geometry.

chapters.headline: SoC4-A is optionality this raise does not fund, not a commitment.
chapters.lede: SoC4-A is a far-horizon chip, 1,024 tiles on a 4 nm process, assembled from published open PULP silicon IP, targeting a Q3 2029 tape-out and packaged into a four-chip, 4U rack-mount box called MicroDC-A1. It sits deliberately outside the current plan: SoC2 is the funded business; SoC4-A is the option that business buys investors.
chapters.detail: The MicroDC-A1 is a conceptual product: one 4U, 19-inch rack-mount chassis housing four SoC4-A chips, each carrying 1,024 tiles on a 4 nm process and drawing 280 W under cold-plate dielectric (3M Novec) cooling. Peak compute is 16.76 PFLOPS FP4 dense (4 chips × 4.19 PFLOPS); sustained throughput is projected at approximately 12 PFLOPS FP4, pending validation in the SoftHier simulator, all numbers are provisional pending first silicon. Memory totals 256 GB LPDDR5X-9600 across the chassis, with an aggregate bandwidth design target of approximately 1.84 TB/s, and network connectivity of 2× 400 GbE plus 2× 100 GbE. The Information Memorandum describes use cases including sovereign-AI inference (the ~12 PFLOPS sustained figure is cited as sufficient for approximately 50 concurrent users on a 70B-parameter LLM, or approximately 200 users on a 13B model), robotaxi fleet compute, and telecom edge inference, all described as conceptual. SoC4-A silicon targets a Q3 2029 tape-out; MicroDC-A1 chassis shipment is indicated as 2030 or later.
